meta.title: Who really said "The world is a book, and those who do not travel read only one page"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not Augustine. Quote Investigator traces the travel line to Richard Lassels's 1670 Voyage of Italy, which credited Augustine only with the world-as-book image.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'The world is a book, and those who do not travel read only one page'?
meta.ogDescription: Not Augustine. The line comes from Richard Lassels's 1670 Voyage of Italy. Augustine called the world a book, but never paired it with travel.

answer.label: Not Augustine of Hippo — actually Richard Lassels
answer.authorDates: c. 1603–1668 · English priest, tutor & travel writer
answer.sourceLine: The travel line comes from the preface to Lassels’s The Voyage of Italy (1670): “They that never stir from home, read only one page of this Book.” Lassels credited Augustine only with calling the world “a great book”. Later compilers gave Augustine the whole sentence, and the familiar wording is a modern condensation.

source.heading: Where the line really comes from

docMeta.dd: The Voyage of Italy, or A Compleat Journey through Italy
A Preface to the Reader Concerning Travelling
Printed at Paris, sold in London by John Starkey, 1670

source.excerpt: … the Profit of Travelling; it’s certain, that if this world be a great book, as S. Augustine calls it, none study this great Book so much as the Traveler. They that never stir from home, read only one page of this Book; and like the dull fellow in Pliny, who could never learn to count farther than five, they dwell alwayes upon one Lesson.
trail: Quote Investigator ↗ found no substantive evidence for Augustine. Its earliest match is the preface to Richard Lassels’s The Voyage of Italy (1670), and it concludes that the Augustine credit came from a misreading of Lassels.
An Internet Archive scan of the 1670 edition ↗ contains the passage: the world as “a great book, as S. Augustine calls it,” and those who never stir from home reading one page of it.
Wikiquote ↗ lists the line among Augustine’s Misattributed quotes and says it has not been found in his writings.
In 1824, Select Proverbs of All Nations ↗ gave the condensed proverb (“The world is a great book, of which they that never stir from home read only a page”) a bare “Augustine” credit.
source.excerptNote: Transcription as given by Quote Investigator. The 1670 print uses period spelling and the long s. Notice that Lassels gives Augustine only the “great book” image. The one-page line is his own.

source.rightsNote: The source passage is from Richard Lassels’s The Voyage of Italy, first published in 1670. That is long before 1931, so it is in the US public domain. The shorter modern wording (“The world is a book, and those who do not travel read only one page”) is an anonymous condensation of Lassels and has no identifiable author of its own.

author.name: Richard Lassels
author.heading: Who Richard Lassels was
author.metaLine: c. 1603–1668 · English Roman Catholic priest, travelling tutor & travel writer
author.bio: Richard Lassels was an English Roman Catholic priest and travel writer. He guided young English nobles through Italy as a tutor and died in Montpellier in 1668. His guide The Voyage of Italy was edited by his fellow priest Simon Wilson and published after his death, in Paris and London in 1670. Wikipedia credits him with coining the term Grand Tour.

misattribution.heading: Why the wrong names stick
misattribution.intro: This saying has been credited to at least five people. Augustine is the most common choice. According to Quote Investigator, the credit grew out of a 1670 sentence that mentioned him by name.

items.why: Augustine did call the world a book. Quote Investigator quotes a letter: “Our greater book is the world; in it I read fulfilled what in the book of God I read promised.” But that passage is about God’s promises, not travel. Lassels cited him for the image alone. According to Quote Investigator ↗, later writers credited Augustine with the whole statement: “A. R.” in 1757, John Feltham in 1799 and Thomas Fielding in 1824.

His Le Cosmopolite, ou le Citoyen du Monde opens with a French version, without attribution: “L’Univers est une espece de livre, dont on n’a lu que la premiere page quand on n’a vu que son Pays” (text at Wikisource ↗). Quote Investigator dates the book to 1750, eighty years after Lassels.

Byron reprinted the Fougeret de Monbron passage, in French, on the title page of Childe Harold’s Pilgrimage. That gave the passage wide circulation, according to Quote Investigator ↗, but Byron was quoting it, not writing it.

A 1907 issue of The Editor credited a version to Stendhal. In 1936 a reader’s letter in the New York Times credited a French version to “Lamartine”. Quote Investigator ↗ found no substantive support for either.

misattribution.truthLine: The person who first wrote the travel line is Richard Lassels, in the preface to The Voyage of Italy (1670). He borrowed only the “world is a book” image from Augustine (Quote Investigator ↗).

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: Lassels wrote for young English gentlemen setting out on what Wikipedia ↗ credits him with naming the Grand Tour. His preface makes the case for “the Profit of Travelling”, and the one-page image is its opening argument: someone who stays home keeps rereading the same lesson.

Naming Augustine in that argument gave it authority. Once the sentence was cut down to a proverb, Augustine’s name stayed attached and Lassels’s fell away. Proverb collections from 1824 onward print it under “Augustine”, and the modern wording has kept that credit.
context.detailsSummary: What Augustine actually meant by “the world as a book”
detailsBody: In the letter that Quote Investigator ↗ cites, Augustine writes “Major liber noster orbis terrarum est”: our greater book is the world, where he reads fulfilled what Scripture promised. The image is about seeing God’s word come true across the world. It does not urge anyone to travel.
WIST ↗ labels the travel version “Spurious” and notes that Augustine did not mean the image as encouragement to travel.

sourcesVerified.claim: QI found no substantive evidence for Augustine. Its earliest match is Lassels, The Voyage of Italy (1670) preface, with the passage text, and it concludes the Augustine credit came from a misreading of Lassels.

QI gives Augustine's letter ("Major liber noster orbis terrarum est" / "Our greater book is the world..."), Fougeret de Monbron's Le Cosmopolite (1750), Byron's 1812 epigraph, A. R. 1757, Feltham 1799, Fielding 1824, Stendhal 1907 and Lamartine 1936.

The 1670 Lassels scan (printed at Paris, sold by John Starkey, 1670) contains 'if this world be a great book, as S. Augustine calls it ... They that never stir from home, read onely one page of this Book' (OCR checked).

Wikiquote's Augustine page lists 'The world is a great book, of which they that never stir from home read only a page' in its Misattributed section and says it has not been located in Augustine's writings.
Select Proverbs of All Nations (1824, Thomas Fielding) prints 'The world is a great book, of which they that never stir from home read only a page.—Augustine.' (OCR checked).
Wikisource's Le Cosmopolite contains 'L'Univers est une espece de livre, dont on n'a lu que la premiere page quand on n'a vu que son Pays'.

Richard Lassels (c. 1603–1668) was a Roman Catholic priest and travel writer who died in 1668. The Voyage of Italy was edited by Simon Wilson and published in Paris/London in 1670, and Lassels coined the term Grand Tour.
WIST labels the Augustine attribution Spurious and says Augustine did not mean the world-as-book image as encouragement to travel.
